# Section A — Solving an equation: roots gained and roots lost

## Question 1 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">TMUA early specimen · P2 Q3</span>

::: {.question}
Consider the following attempt to solve an equation. The steps have been numbered for reference.

$$\sqrt{x+5}=x+3$$
$$\text{step (1)}\ \big\downarrow$$
$$x+5=x^{2}+6x+9$$
$$\text{step (2)}\ \big\downarrow$$
$$x^{2}+5x+4=0$$
$$\text{step (3)}\ \big\downarrow$$
$$(x+4)(x+1)=0$$
$$x=-4\ \text{ or }\ x=-1$$

Which one of the following statements is true?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** Both $-4$ and $-1$ are solutions of the equation.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** Neither $-4$ nor $-1$ are solutions of the equation.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** One solution is correct and the incorrect solution arises as a result of step (1).

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** One solution is correct and the incorrect solution arises as a result of step (2).

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** One solution is correct and the incorrect solution arises as a result of step (3).
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**C.**

**Step 1 — Test both values in the original equation.** This settles options A and B at once.

- $x=-4$: the left side is $\sqrt{1}=1$ and the right side is $-4+3=-1$. These differ, so $-4$ is **not** a
  solution.
- $x=-1$: the left side is $\sqrt{4}=2$ and the right side is $-1+3=2$. So $-1$ **is** a solution.

So exactly one value is correct, which removes A and B.

**Step 2 — Find where $x=-4$ enters.** Put $x=-4$ into each line in turn.

- Original line: $1=-1$, false.
- After step (1): $x+5=1$ and $x^{2}+6x+9=16-24+9=1$, so the line reads $1=1$, true.

The value $-4$ fails before step (1) and works after it, so step (1) is where it came in.

**Step 3 — Why D and E fail.** Steps (2) and (3) are a rearrangement and a factorisation. Each keeps exactly
the same solutions, so neither can introduce anything.

**The idea.** Squaring turns $-1=1$ into the true $1=1$. That is how a false value survives.
:::

---

## Question 2 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">Notes on Logic and Proof · Exercise Q</span>

::: {.question}
Solve: $\;\sqrt{2x+3}+\sqrt{x+1}=\sqrt{7x+4}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**$x=3$ is the only solution.**

**Step 1 — Square both sides.** The left side is a sum, so a middle term appears:

$$(2x+3)+2\sqrt{(2x+3)(x+1)}+(x+1)=7x+4 .$$

**Step 2 — Isolate the remaining root.** Collect the terms without a root:

$$2\sqrt{(2x+3)(x+1)}=7x+4-3x-4=4x ,$$

and halve:

$$\sqrt{(2x+3)(x+1)}=2x .$$

**Step 3 — Square again.**

$$(2x+3)(x+1)=4x^{2}$$
$$2x^{2}+5x+3=4x^{2}$$
$$2x^{2}-5x-3=0$$
$$(2x+1)(x-3)=0 .$$

So the candidates are $x=-\tfrac12$ and $x=3$.

**Step 4 — Check each candidate in the original.** Squaring is one-way, so these are only candidates.

- $x=3$: $\sqrt9+\sqrt4=3+2=5$ and $\sqrt{25}=5$. ✓
- $x=-\tfrac12$: $\sqrt2+\sqrt{\tfrac12}$ against $\sqrt{\tfrac12}$. These differ by $\sqrt2$. ✗

**The tell.** Step 2 already gave it away: a square root is never negative, so $\sqrt{\;\cdot\;}=2x$ forces
$x\ge0$, and $x=-\tfrac12$ was never possible.
:::

---

## Question 3 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2018 · P2 Q9</span>

::: {.question}
Consider the following attempt to solve the equation $4x\sqrt{2x-1}=10x-5$:

$$4x\sqrt{2x-1}=10x-5$$
$$\text{(I)}\ \big\downarrow$$
$$4x\sqrt{2x-1}=5(2x-1)$$
$$\text{(II)}\ \big\downarrow$$
$$16x^{2}(2x-1)=25(2x-1)^{2}$$
$$\text{(III)}\ \big\downarrow$$
$$16x^{2}=25(2x-1)$$
$$\text{(IV)}\ \big\downarrow$$
$$16x^{2}-50x+25=0$$
$$\text{(V)}\ \big\downarrow$$
$$(8x-5)(2x-5)=0$$
$$\text{(VI)}\ \big\downarrow$$
$$\text{The solutions of the original equation are } x=\tfrac58 \text{ and } x=\tfrac52.$$

Which one of the following is true?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** The solution is correct.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** Only one of $x=\tfrac58$ and $x=\tfrac52$ is correct and the error arises as a result of step (II).

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** Only one of $x=\tfrac58$ and $x=\tfrac52$ is correct and the error arises as a result of step (III).

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** Only one of $x=\tfrac58$ and $x=\tfrac52$ is correct and the error arises as a result of step (IV).

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** There is another value of $x$ that satisfies the original equation and the error arises as a result of step (II).

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** There is another value of $x$ that satisfies the original equation and the error arises as a result of step (III).

&nbsp;&nbsp;**G** There is another value of $x$ that satisfies the original equation and the error arises as a result of step (IV).
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**F.**

**Step 1 — Test the two answers given.**

- $x=\tfrac58$: the left side is $4\cdot\tfrac58\cdot\sqrt{\tfrac14}=\tfrac54$ and the right side is
  $\tfrac{25}{4}-5=\tfrac54$. ✓
- $x=\tfrac52$: the left side is $4\cdot\tfrac52\cdot\sqrt{4}=20$ and the right side is $25-5=20$. ✓

Both are correct, so B, C and D are out.

**Step 2 — Look for a step that could lose a solution.** Squaring at step (II) can only add solutions, and here
it added none. Step (III) is different: it **divides both sides by $(2x-1)$**, and that bracket is zero at
$x=\tfrac12$.

**Step 3 — Test $x=\tfrac12$ in the original.** The left side is $4\cdot\tfrac12\cdot\sqrt0=0$ and the right
side is $5-5=0$. So $x=\tfrac12$ is a genuine solution, and step (III) threw it away. That is **F**.

**The repair.** Do not divide. From $16x^{2}(2x-1)=25(2x-1)^{2}$, bring everything to one side and factorise:

$$(2x-1)\big(16x^{2}-25(2x-1)\big)=0 ,$$

which gives $x=\tfrac12,\ \tfrac58,\ \tfrac52$. All three check.
:::

## Question 4 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2017 · P2 Q4</span>

::: {.question}
The following question appeared in an examination:

> Given that $\tan x=\sqrt3$, find the possible values of $\sin 2x$.

A student gave the following answer:

> $\tan x=\sqrt3$ so $x=60^\circ$ and $2x=120^\circ$, therefore $\sin 2x=\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$.

Which one of the following statements is correct?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** $\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$ is the only possible value, and this is fully supported by the reasoning given in the student's answer.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** $\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$ is the only possible value, but the reasoning given should consider other possible values of $x$ for which $\tan x=\sqrt3$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** $\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$ is the only possible value, but the reasoning given should consider other possible values of $x$ for which $\sin 2x=\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** $\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$ is **not** the only possible value because the reasoning given should have considered other possible values of $x$ for which $\tan x=\sqrt3$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** $\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$ is **not** the only possible value because the reasoning given should have considered other possible values of $x$ for which $\sin 2x=\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**B.** Two separate questions are being asked: what is the true set of values, and was the reasoning complete?

**Step 1 — Find every $x$.** The student stops at $x=60^\circ$, but $\tan$ repeats every $180^\circ$, so

$$\tan x=\sqrt3\iff x=60^\circ+180^\circ n\quad\text{for an integer }n .$$

So the reasoning is incomplete, which rules out A.

**Step 2 — Find every value of $\sin 2x$.** Doubling gives $2x=120^\circ+360^\circ n$. Since $\sin$ repeats every
$360^\circ$,

$$\sin 2x=\sin 120^\circ=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\quad\text{for every }n .$$

So there is only one possible value, which rules out D and E.

**Step 3 — Choose between B and C.** The values the student had to consider come from the **given** equation
$\tan x=\sqrt3$. Starting from $\sin 2x=\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$, as in C, would use the answer to find the answer, and
it would also admit values such as $2x=60^\circ$, where $\tan x\ne\sqrt3$.

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "tan x meets the line y = √3 at 60° and at 240°. At both of these x, sin 2x takes the same value."
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig, (a1, a2) = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(6.4, 6.0))
x = np.linspace(0, 360, 2000)
y = np.tan(np.radians(x)); y[np.abs(y) > 8] = np.nan
a1.plot(x, y, color='#1f77b4', lw=2)
a1.axhline(np.sqrt(3), color='#d62728', ls='--', lw=1.5)
for v in (60, 240):
    a1.plot(v, np.sqrt(3), 'o', color='#d62728')
    a1.annotate(f'{v}°', (v, np.sqrt(3)), textcoords='offset points', xytext=(-16, 8), color='#d62728')
a1.set_ylim(-6, 6); a1.set_xlim(0, 360); a1.set_xticks(range(0, 361, 60)); a1.grid(alpha=.25)
a1.set_title(r'$y=\tan x$ and $y=\sqrt{3}$', fontsize=11)
a2.plot(x, np.sin(np.radians(2 * x)), color='#2ca02c', lw=2)
for v in (60, 240):
    a2.plot(v, np.sqrt(3) / 2, 'o', color='#d62728')
    a2.annotate(f'{v}°', (v, np.sqrt(3) / 2), textcoords='offset points', xytext=(0, 8), ha='center', color='#d62728')
a2.set_xlim(0, 360); a2.set_ylim(-1.3, 1.4); a2.set_xticks(range(0, 361, 60)); a2.grid(alpha=.25)
a2.set_xlabel('x (degrees)'); a2.set_title(r'$y=\sin 2x$', fontsize=11)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

**The idea.** A right answer does not mean right reasoning. On this kind of question, judge the two separately.
:::

## Question 5 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2019 · P2 Q6</span>

::: {.question}
A student attempts to solve the equation

$$\cos x+\sin x\tan x=2\sin x-1$$

in the range $0\le x\le 2\pi$. The student's attempt is as follows:

$$\cos x+\sin x\tan x=2\sin x-1$$

So $\;\cos x-\sin x+\sin x\tan x-\sin x=-1$ &nbsp;&nbsp;**(I)**

So $\;(\sin x-\cos x)(\tan x-1)=-1$ &nbsp;&nbsp;**(II)**

So $\;\sin x-\cos x=-1\;$ or $\;\tan x-1=-1$ &nbsp;&nbsp;**(III)**

So $\;(\sin x-\cos x)^{2}=1\;$ or $\;\tan x=0$ &nbsp;&nbsp;**(IV)**

So $\;2\sin x\cos x=0\;$ or $\;\tan x=0$ &nbsp;&nbsp;**(V)**

So $\;x=0,\ \tfrac{\pi}{2},\ \pi,\ \tfrac{3\pi}{2},\ 2\pi$ &nbsp;&nbsp;**(VI)**

Which of the following best describes this attempt?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** It is completely correct

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** It is incorrect, and the first error occurs on line (I)

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** It is incorrect, and the first error occurs on line (II)

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** It is incorrect, and the first error occurs on line (III)

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** It is incorrect, and the first error is that extra solutions were introduced on line (IV)

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** It is incorrect, and the first error is that extra solutions were introduced on line (V)

&nbsp;&nbsp;**G** It is incorrect, and the first error is not eliminating the values where $\tan x$ is undefined on line (VI)
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**D.** Test a wrong final answer to locate the fault.

**Step 1 — The final list is wrong.** At $x=0$ the left side of the original is $\cos0+0=1$ and the right side
is $0-1=-1$. So $x=0$ is not a solution, and A fails. Since $\tan0$ is defined, this failure is not about
undefined values, so G is not the first error either.

**Step 2 — Check the early lines.**

- Line (I) subtracts $2\sin x$ from both sides. ✓
- Line (II): multiplying out,
$$(\sin x-\cos x)(\tan x-1)=\sin x\tan x-\sin x-\cos x\tan x+\cos x .$$
  Since $\cos x\tan x=\sin x$, this equals $\cos x-\sin x+\sin x\tan x-\sin x$, which is line (I). ✓

**Step 3 — Line (III) is the leap.** It says that if two numbers multiply to give $-1$, then one of them must be
$-1$. That reasoning works for a product equal to **zero**. It fails for $-1$, because $2\times(-\tfrac12)=-1$
and neither factor is $-1$.

**Step 4 — Confirm with $x=0$.** Line (II) at $x=0$ gives $(-1)(-1)=1\neq-1$, so it is false there. Line (III) at
$x=0$ gives $-1=-1$, so it is true. A value that fails line (II) passes line (III), so line (III) does not follow.

**Why E and F fail.** Those lines do widen the solution set, but they come after line (III), and the question
asks for the **first** error.
:::

# Section B — Inequalities and signs

## Question 6 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">Notes on Logic and Proof · Exercise R, Q3</span>

::: {.question}
Starting with $\dfrac{x+2}{2x+7}<5$, is it then valid to deduce $x+2<5(2x+7)$? Justify your answer.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**No, the deduction is not valid.**

**Step 1 — What the step does.** It multiplies both sides by $2x+7$. The direction of an inequality is kept only
if the multiplier is positive, and $2x+7$ is negative whenever $x<-\tfrac72$.

**Step 2 — A value that breaks it.** Take $x=-4$, so that $2x+7=-1$.

- The starting inequality: $\dfrac{-2}{-1}=2<5$. True.
- The deduced inequality: $x+2=-2$ and $5(2x+7)=-5$, and $-2<-5$ is false.

A true starting line has given a false next line, so the step is invalid.

**Step 3 — The safe move.** Multiply by $(2x+7)^{2}$, which is positive for every $x\ne-\tfrac72$:

$$(x+2)(2x+7)<5(2x+7)^{2}$$
$$(2x+7)\big(5(2x+7)-(x+2)\big)>0$$
$$(2x+7)(9x+33)>0 .$$

This gives $x<-\tfrac{11}{3}$ or $x>-\tfrac72$. Our value $x=-4$ lies in the first part, as it should.
:::

---

## Question 7 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">Notes on Logic and Proof · Exercise R, Q1</span>

::: {.question}
Given $x<y$, what positive integer values of $n$ make $x^{n}<y^{n}$ true?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**Exactly the odd values of $n$,** for all real $x<y$.

**Step 1 — Even $n$ can fail.** Take $x=-2$ and $y=1$, so $x<y$. For any even $n$,

$$x^{n}=(-2)^{n}=2^{n}\ge4>1=y^{n} .$$

So $x^{n}<y^{n}$ is false for every even $n$ with this one pair. (It does hold when $x$ and $y$ are both
non-negative, but the question does not give us that.)

**Step 2 — Odd $n$ always works.** The function $t\mapsto t^{n}$ with $n$ odd is strictly increasing on the whole
real line, so a larger input always gives a larger output. The graphs below show the difference.

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "y = x² fails the horizontal line test, so order is not kept. y = x³ is increasing everywhere, so order is kept."
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig, (a1, a2) = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(6.0, 6.2))
x = np.linspace(-2.4, 2.4, 500)
a1.plot(x, x**2, color='#1f77b4', lw=2)
a1.plot([-2, 1], [4, 1], 'o', color='#d62728')
a1.annotate('x = −2, output 4', (-2, 4), textcoords='offset points', xytext=(12, 2), color='#d62728')
a1.annotate('y = 1, output 1', (1, 1), textcoords='offset points', xytext=(10, -4), color='#d62728')
a1.axhline(0, color='0.6', lw=.8); a1.axvline(0, color='0.6', lw=.8); a1.grid(alpha=.25)
a1.set_title(r'$n=2$: $-2<1$ but $(-2)^2>1^2$', fontsize=11)
a2.plot(x, x**3, color='#2ca02c', lw=2)
a2.plot([-2, 1], [-8, 1], 'o', color='#d62728')
a2.annotate('x = −2, output −8', (-2, -8), textcoords='offset points', xytext=(12, 2), color='#d62728')
a2.annotate('y = 1, output 1', (1, 1), textcoords='offset points', xytext=(10, -6), color='#d62728')
a2.axhline(0, color='0.6', lw=.8); a2.axvline(0, color='0.6', lw=.8); a2.grid(alpha=.25)
a2.set_title(r'$n=3$: $-2<1$ and $(-2)^3<1^3$', fontsize=11)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

**The idea.** Applying a function to both sides of an inequality is safe only if the function is increasing on
all the values in play.
:::

---

## Question 8 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">Tyler TMUA Set C · P2 Q3</span>

::: {.question}
The real numbers $a$, $b$ and $c$ are non-zero and $a\le b$.

Which of the following statements are necessarily true?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I** $\;\dfrac1a\ge\dfrac1b$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**II** $\;2^{a}\le2^{b}$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**III** $\;ac\le bc$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** none of them

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** I only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** II only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** I and II only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** II and III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**G** I and III only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**H** I, II and III
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**C.** Test each statement separately, looking for a counterexample.

**I is false.** The reciprocal rule needs $a$ and $b$ to have the same sign. Take $a=-2$ and $b=1$. Then
$\tfrac1a=-\tfrac12$ and $\tfrac1b=1$, and $-\tfrac12\ge1$ is false.

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "y = 1/x has a break at x = 0. Going from a = −2 to b = 1 crosses it, so the order of the outputs does not reverse."
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.6, 3.8))
x1 = np.linspace(-4, -0.2, 300); x2 = np.linspace(0.2, 4, 300)
ax.plot(x1, 1 / x1, color='#1f77b4', lw=2); ax.plot(x2, 1 / x2, color='#1f77b4', lw=2)
ax.plot([-2, 1], [-0.5, 1], 'o', color='#d62728')
ax.annotate('a = −2, 1/a = −1/2', (-2, -0.5), textcoords='offset points', xytext=(-30, 12), color='#d62728')
ax.annotate('b = 1, 1/b = 1', (1, 1), textcoords='offset points', xytext=(10, 6), color='#d62728')
ax.axhline(0, color='0.6', lw=.8); ax.axvline(0, color='0.6', lw=.8); ax.set_ylim(-5, 5); ax.grid(alpha=.25)
ax.set_xlabel('x'); ax.set_ylabel('y')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

**II is true.** $y=2^{x}$ is an increasing function, so $a\le b$ gives $2^{a}\le2^{b}$ for every $a$ and $b$.

**III is false.** The sign of $c$ is unknown. Take $a=1$, $b=2$, $c=-1$. Then $ac=-1$ and $bc=-2$, and
$-1\le-2$ is false.

So only II must hold.
:::

---

## Question 9 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2016 · P2 Q8</span>

::: {.question}
A region is defined by the inequalities $x+y>6$ and $x-y>-4$.

Consider the three statements:

&nbsp;&nbsp;**1** $\;x>1$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**2** $\;y>5$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**3** $\;(x+y)(x-y)>-24$

Which of the above statements is/are true for **every** point in the region?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** none

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** 1 only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** 2 only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** 3 only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** 1 and 2 only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** 1 and 3 only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**G** 2 and 3 only

&nbsp;&nbsp;**H** 1, 2 and 3
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**B.**

**Statement 1 is true.** Two inequalities pointing the same way may always be added:

$$(x+y)+(x-y)>6+(-4)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad 2x>2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x>1 .$$

**Statement 2 is false.** Take $(x,y)=(10,0)$. Then $x+y=10>6$ and $x-y=10>-4$, so the point is in the region,
but $y=0$ is not greater than $5$.

**Statement 3 is false.** It is what you get by multiplying the two given inequalities, $6\times(-4)=-24$. That
step is not allowed, because $x-y$ can be negative. Take $(x,y)=(3.05,\,6.95)$:

$$x+y=10>6,\qquad x-y=-3.9>-4,\qquad (x+y)(x-y)=-39 ,$$

and $-39$ is not greater than $-24$.

```{python}
#| fig-cap: "The region is the wedge with apex (1, 5). Every point has x > 1. The marked point is in the wedge but makes (x+y)(x−y) = −39."
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt
x = np.linspace(-1, 12, 400)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.6, 4.0))
ax.plot(x, -x + 6, color='#1f77b4', lw=2, label='x + y = 6')
ax.plot(x, x + 4, color='#dd6b20', lw=2, label='x − y = −4')
low = np.maximum(-x + 6, -2)
ax.fill_between(x, low, x + 4, where=(x + 4 > low), color='#2ca02c', alpha=.12)
ax.plot(1, 5, 'o', color='k'); ax.annotate('apex (1, 5)', (1, 5), (1.4, 2.6), fontsize=9)
ax.plot(3.05, 6.95, 'o', color='#d62728')
ax.annotate('(3.05, 6.95)', (3.05, 6.95), (3.4, 9.0), fontsize=9, color='#d62728')
ax.axhline(0, color='0.6', lw=.6); ax.axvline(0, color='0.6', lw=.6)
ax.set_xlim(-1, 12); ax.set_ylim(-2, 12); ax.legend(fontsize=8, loc='lower right')
ax.set_xlabel('x'); ax.set_ylabel('y')
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

**The idea.** Multiplying inequalities needs every quantity to be positive. Here the second bracket is only known
to be above $-4$.
:::

## Question 10 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2023 · P2 Q10</span>

::: {.question}
Here is an attempt to solve the inequality $x^{4}-2x^{2}-3<0$ by completing the square:

$$x^{4}-2x^{2}-3<0$$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I** &nbsp; if and only if $x^{4}-2x^{2}+1<4$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**II** &nbsp; if and only if $(x^{2}-1)^{2}<4$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**III** &nbsp; if and only if $-2<x^{2}-1<2$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**IV** &nbsp; if and only if $x^{2}-1<2$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**V** &nbsp; if and only if $x^{2}<3$

&nbsp;&nbsp;**VI** &nbsp; if and only if $-\sqrt3<x<\sqrt3$

Which of the following statements is true?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** The argument is completely correct.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** The first error occurs in line I.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** The first error occurs in line II.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** The first error occurs in line III.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** The first error occurs in line IV.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** The first error occurs in line V.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**G** The first error occurs in line VI.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**A.** Every line claims "if and only if", so each must work in both directions.

**Step 1 — Lines I to III.** Line I adds $4$ to both sides. Line II uses $x^{4}-2x^{2}+1=(x^{2}-1)^{2}$. Line III
uses $u^{2}<4\iff-2<u<2$ with $u=x^{2}-1$. All three are genuine equivalences.

**Step 2 — The suspicious line IV.** It drops the half "$-2<x^{2}-1$". Dropping a condition can change a solution
set, so check it. Since $x^{2}\ge0$, we always have $x^{2}-1\ge-1>-2$. The dropped half is true for **every** $x$,
so removing it changes nothing.

**Step 3 — Lines V and VI.** Line V adds $1$. Line VI is $x^{2}<3\iff\lvert x\rvert<\sqrt3$. Both are fine.

**Step 4 — An independent check.** Factorise the original:

$$x^{4}-2x^{2}-3=(x^{2}-3)(x^{2}+1) .$$

Since $x^{2}+1>0$, this is negative exactly when $x^{2}<3$. The answer agrees.

**The idea.** Not every question of this type contains an error. Being suspicious is right; you still need a
value that actually breaks the line.
:::

---

# Section C — Proofs that do not hold up

## Question 11 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">Tyler TMUA Set C · P2 Q5</span>

::: {.question}
A student attempts to prove the following statement.

> Consider the integers $a$ and $b$, where $a$ has remainder $1$ when divided by $3$, and $b$ has remainder $2$
> when divided by $3$. Then $a+b$ is always divisible by $3$.

Consider the following attempt:

&nbsp;&nbsp;Let $a=3n+1$ and $b=3n+2$ &nbsp;&nbsp;**(I)**

&nbsp;&nbsp;then $\;a+b=3n+1+3n+2$ &nbsp;&nbsp;**(II)**

&nbsp;&nbsp;so $\;a+b=6n+3$ &nbsp;&nbsp;**(III)**

&nbsp;&nbsp;so $\;a+b=3(2n+1)$ &nbsp;&nbsp;**(IV)**

&nbsp;&nbsp;therefore $a+b$ is always divisible by $3$. &nbsp;&nbsp;**(V)**

Which of the following best describes this proof?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** The statement is true and the proof is completely correct.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** The statement is true but there is an error in the proof in line (I)

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** The statement is true but there is an error in the proof in line (II)

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** The statement is not true and there is an error in the proof in line (III)

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** The statement is not true and there is an error in the proof in line (IV)

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** The statement is not true and there is an error in the proof in line (V)
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**B.**

**Step 1 — Is the statement true?** Yes. Remainders $1$ and $2$ add to $3$. This removes D, E and F.

**Step 2 — What line (I) assumes.** Using the same letter $n$ in both says that $a$ and $b$ have the **same**
quotient on division by $3$. That is an extra assumption. For example $a=1$ and $b=5$ satisfy the statement, with
quotients $0$ and $1$, and line (I) cannot describe that pair. So the proof only covers pairs such as $a=4,\ b=5$.

**Step 3 — The repair.** Use two letters: $a=3n+1$ and $b=3m+2$. Then

$$a+b=3n+3m+3=3(n+m+1) ,$$

which is divisible by $3$. Lines (II) to (V) all follow correctly from line (I), so the first error is line (I).

**The idea.** A new unknown needs a new letter. Reusing one quietly proves a smaller statement.
:::

---

## Question 12 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">Tyler TMUA Set D · P2 Q7</span>

::: {.question}
A student attempts to prove that there are infinitely many prime numbers as follows:

&nbsp;&nbsp;Assume that there are finitely many prime numbers, and let the largest be $p$ &nbsp;&nbsp;**(I)**

&nbsp;&nbsp;Let $n=2p+1$ so that $n>p$ &nbsp;&nbsp;**(II)**

&nbsp;&nbsp;Consider $n=2p+1$. This is not divisible by $p$ &nbsp;&nbsp;**(III)**

&nbsp;&nbsp;Therefore $n$ is also a prime number &nbsp;&nbsp;**(IV)**

&nbsp;&nbsp;This contradicts the initial assumption so we conclude that there are infinitely many prime numbers
&nbsp;&nbsp;**(V)**

Which of the following best describes this proof?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** The statement is not true and there is an error in the proof in line (I)

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** The statement is not true and there is an error in the proof in line (II)

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** The statement is true but there is an error in the proof in line (III)

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** The statement is true but there is an error in the proof in line (IV)

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** The statement is true but there is an error in the proof in line (V)

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** The statement is true and the proof is completely correct.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**D.**

**Step 1 — The statement is true.** There are infinitely many primes, so A and B are out.

**Step 2 — Check lines (I) to (III).** Line (I) sets up a proof by contradiction. Line (II) holds since $2p+1>p$.
Line (III) holds since $2p+1$ leaves remainder $1$ on division by $p$, because $p\ge2$.

**Step 3 — Line (IV) is the false step.** Not being divisible by $p$ does not make $n$ prime. It could be divisible
by a smaller prime. Take $p=7$: then $n=15=3\times5$, which is not divisible by $7$ and is not prime.

**Why E fails.** Line (V) would follow if line (IV) were true, so it is not the first error.

**The repair.** Euclid's proof uses $n=$ (the product of all the primes) $+1$. That leaves remainder $1$ on division
by **every** prime, not just by $p$.
:::

---

## Question 13 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">Notes on Logic and Proof · Exercise K, Q5</span>

::: {.question}
Why is it a mistake to write the contrapositive of

> if $a$ and $b$ are odd, then $ab$ is odd

as

> if $ab$ is not odd then $a$ and $b$ are not odd?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**Because the negation of "$a$ and $b$ are odd" is not "$a$ and $b$ are not odd".**

**Step 1 — Write the two halves.** The hypothesis is an **and**: "$a$ is odd **and** $b$ is odd".

**Step 2 — Negate it correctly.** The negation of "$P$ and $Q$" is "not $P$ **or** not $Q$":

$$\text{not}(a\text{ odd and }b\text{ odd})\ =\ a\text{ is even or }b\text{ is even}.$$

So the true contrapositive is:

> if $ab$ is even then $a$ and $b$ are not both odd, that is, at least one of $a$ and $b$ is even.

**Step 3 — The careless version is false.** It read "$a$ and $b$ are not odd" as both of them being even. Take
$a=2$ and $b=3$. Then $ab=6$ is not odd, but $b$ is odd. A true statement must have a true contrapositive, so this
cannot be its contrapositive.
:::

---

## Question 14 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">Notes on Logic and Proof · Exercise O, Q1</span>

::: {.question}
Here is the proof that $\sqrt2$ is irrational.

> We assume that $\sqrt2$ is rational. Then it can be written as a fraction in its lowest terms, $\sqrt2=\dfrac ab$,
> where $a$ and $b$ have no factors in common. Squaring both sides gives $2=\dfrac{a^{2}}{b^{2}}$, which gives
> $2b^{2}=a^{2}$. From this we can see that $a^{2}$ is even. For $a^{2}$ to be even, $a$ itself must be even. And if
> $a$ is even then $a^{2}$ is divisible by $4$. If $a^{2}$ is divisible by $4$ then $b^{2}$ must also be even. For
> $b^{2}$ to be even, $b$ must be even. Thus, we have $a$ is even and $b$ is even. This contradicts the assumption
> that $\dfrac ab$ is a fraction in its lowest terms.

Replace $2$ by $9$ in the proof that $\sqrt2$ is irrational. Why does the proof no longer work?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**Because "$a^{2}$ is a multiple of $9$" does not force "$a$ is a multiple of $9$".** It must fail somewhere, since
$\sqrt9=3$ is rational.

**Step 1 — Run the proof with $9$.** From $\sqrt9=\tfrac ab$ in lowest terms we get $9b^{2}=a^{2}$, so $a^{2}$ is a
multiple of $9$.

**Step 2 — The step that breaks.** The proof for $2$ says "for $a^{2}$ to be even, $a$ must be even". That relies on
$2$ being prime. The version for $9$ is false: $a=3$ has $a^{2}=9$, a multiple of $9$, but $3$ is not a multiple of
$9$.

**Step 3 — What really follows.** All we may say is that $a$ is a multiple of $3$. Write $a=3k$. Then

$$9b^{2}=9k^{2}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad b^{2}=k^{2}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad b=k$$

for positive $a$ and $b$. So $a=3b$, which is exactly $\sqrt9=3$. Nothing forces $b$ to share a factor with $a$, and
indeed $\tfrac31$ is in lowest terms. So there is no contradiction.
:::

---

## Question 15 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2020 · P2 Q8</span>

::: {.question}
A student is asked to prove whether the following statement $(*)$ is true or false:

$$(*)\quad\text{For all real numbers } a \text{ and } b,\quad |a+b|<|a|+|b|$$

The student's proof is as follows:

> Statement $(*)$ is false. A counterexample is $a=3$, $b=4$, as $|3+4|=7$ and $|3|+|4|=7$, but $7<7$ is false.

Which of the following best describes the student's proof?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** The statement $(*)$ is true, and the student's proof is not correct.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** The statement $(*)$ is false, but the student's proof is not correct: the counterexample is not valid.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** The statement $(*)$ is false, but the student's proof is not correct: the student needs to give *all* the values of $a$ and $b$ where $|a+b|<|a|+|b|$ is false.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** The statement $(*)$ is false, but the student's proof is not correct: the student should have instead stated that for all real numbers $a$ and $b$, $|a+b|\le|a|+|b|$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** The statement $(*)$ is false, and the student's proof is fully correct.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**E.**

**Step 1 — Is $(*)$ false?** It claims a **strict** inequality for all $a$ and $b$. When $a$ and $b$ have the same sign
the two sides are equal, so it fails. This removes A.

**Step 2 — Is the counterexample valid?** With $a=3$ and $b=4$, $|a+b|=7$ and $|a|+|b|=7$. "$7<7$" is false. So this
pair really does break $(*)$, which removes B. Equality counts as a failure of "$<$".

**Step 3 — Is one enough?** Yes. One case disproves a "for all" statement, so C is wrong.

**Step 4 — Did the student need to repair the statement?** No. They were asked whether it is true or false. The
inequality with "$\le$" is a true fact, but it is not needed, so D is wrong.

**The idea.** The honest answer can be "this proof is fine", even in a question that seems to invite an objection.
:::

---

## Question 16 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2023 · P2 Q4</span>

::: {.question}
A student attempts to answer the following question.

> What is the largest number of consecutive odd integers that are all prime?

The student's attempt is as follows:

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I** &nbsp; There are two consecutive odd integers that are prime (for example: $17,\,19$).

&nbsp;&nbsp;**II** &nbsp; Any three consecutive odd integers can be written in the form $n-2,\ n,\ n+2$ for some $n$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**III** &nbsp; If $n$ is one more than a multiple of $3$, then $n+2$ is a multiple of $3$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**IV** &nbsp; If $n$ is two more than a multiple of $3$, then $n-2$ is a multiple of $3$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**V** &nbsp; The only other possibility is that $n$ is a multiple of $3$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**VI** &nbsp; In each case, one of the integers is a multiple of $3$, so not prime.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**VII** &nbsp; Therefore the largest number of consecutive odd integers that are all prime is two.

Which of the following best describes this attempt?

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** It is completely correct.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** It is incorrect, and the first error is on line I.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** It is incorrect, and the first error is on line II.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** It is incorrect, and the first error is on line III.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** It is incorrect, and the first error is on line IV.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** It is incorrect, and the first error is on line V.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**G** It is incorrect, and the first error is on line VI.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**H** It is incorrect, and the first error is on line VII.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**G.**

**Step 1 — Try small numbers first.** Write out the odd numbers: $1,3,5,7,9,11,\dots$ The run $3,5,7$ is three
consecutive odd integers that are all prime. So the conclusion "two" is false, which rules out A.

**Step 2 — Check lines I to V.**

- Line I: $17$ and $19$ are both prime. ✓
- Line II: consecutive odd integers differ by $2$. ✓
- Line III: if $n=3k+1$ then $n+2=3k+3=3(k+1)$. ✓
- Line IV: if $n=3k+2$ then $n-2=3k$. ✓
- Line V: every integer leaves remainder $0$, $1$ or $2$. ✓

**Step 3 — Line VI is the first false line.** "A multiple of $3$, so not prime" forgets that $3$ itself is a multiple
of $3$ and **is** prime. In the triple $3,5,7$ the multiple of $3$ is $3$.

**Why H fails.** Line VII is false too, but it is not the first false line.

**The idea.** Test the smallest allowed values before you trust a general argument.
:::

---

## Question 17 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">MAT 2022 · Q1G</span>

::: {.question}
For all real $n$, it is the case that $n^{4}+1=\left(n^{2}+\sqrt2\,n+1\right)\left(n^{2}-\sqrt2\,n+1\right)$. From this
we may deduce that $n^{4}+4$ is

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(a)** never a prime number for any positive whole number $n$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(b)** a prime number for exactly one positive whole number $n$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(c)** a prime number for exactly two positive whole numbers $n$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(d)** a prime number for exactly three positive whole numbers $n$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**(e)** a prime number for exactly four positive whole numbers $n$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**(b).**

**Step 1 — Use the given identity.** It holds for all real $n$, so replace $n$ by $\dfrac{m}{\sqrt2}$:

$$\frac{m^{4}}{4}+1=\left(\frac{m^{2}}{2}+m+1\right)\left(\frac{m^{2}}{2}-m+1\right).$$

Multiply both sides by $4$, giving a factor of $2$ to each bracket:

$$m^{4}+4=\left(m^{2}+2m+2\right)\left(m^{2}-2m+2\right).$$

**Step 2 — When can a product be prime?** Both factors are positive integers when $m$ is a positive whole number. A
product of two positive integers is prime only if one factor is $1$.

**Step 3 — Find when a factor equals $1$.** The smaller factor is

$$m^{2}-2m+2=(m-1)^{2}+1 ,$$

which equals $1$ only at $m=1$. The larger factor is at least $5$ for $m\ge1$.

**Step 4 — Check.** At $m=1$, $m^{4}+4=5$, which is prime. For $m\ge2$ both factors exceed $1$, so the value is
composite. For example $2^{4}+4=20=2\times10$. So $n^{4}+4$ is prime for exactly one positive whole number.

**The idea.** Do not stop at "it factorises, so it is never prime". That line is the same kind of error as the ones
on this sheet, and it leads to option (a).
:::

---

## Question 18 &nbsp;<span style="font-size:0.72em;color:#8a8a8a;font-weight:400">2017 · P2 Q9</span>

::: {.question}
Consider the following attempt to prove this true theorem:

> *Theorem:* $a^{3}+b^{3}=c^{3}$ has no solutions with $a$, $b$ and $c$ positive integers.

*Attempted proof:* Suppose that there are positive integers $a$, $b$ and $c$ such that $a^{3}+b^{3}=c^{3}$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**I** &nbsp; We have $a^{3}=c^{3}-b^{3}$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**II** &nbsp; Hence $a^{3}=(c-b)(c^{2}+cb+b^{2})$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**III** &nbsp; It follows that $a=c-b$ and $a^{2}=c^{2}+cb+b^{2}$, since $a\leqslant a^{2}$ and
$c-b\leqslant c^{2}+cb+b^{2}$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**IV** &nbsp; Eliminating $a$, we have $(c-b)^{2}=c^{2}+cb+b^{2}$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**V** &nbsp; Multiplying out, we have $c^{2}-2cb+b^{2}=c^{2}+cb+b^{2}$.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**VI** &nbsp; Hence $3cb=0$ so one of $b$ and $c$ is zero.

But this is a contradiction to the original assumption that all of $a$, $b$ and $c$ are positive. It follows that the
equation has no solutions.

Comment on this proof by choosing one of the following options:

&nbsp;&nbsp;**A** The proof is correct

&nbsp;&nbsp;**B** The proof is incorrect and the first mistake occurs on line I.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**C** The proof is incorrect and the first mistake occurs on line II.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**D** The proof is incorrect and the first mistake occurs on line III.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**E** The proof is incorrect and the first mistake occurs on line IV.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**F** The proof is incorrect and the first mistake occurs on line V.

&nbsp;&nbsp;**G** The proof is incorrect and the first mistake occurs on line VI.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Solution

**D.**

**Step 1 — Lines I and II are fine.** Line I rearranges the equation. Line II is the standard difference of two
cubes.

**Step 2 — What line III claims.** We have $a\cdot a^{2}=(c-b)(c^{2}+cb+b^{2})$, and in each product the first factor
is the smaller. Line III concludes that the factors must match, smaller with smaller.

**Step 3 — Why that does not follow.** A number can be written as a product in many ways. Take $a=6$:

$$6^{3}=216=6\times36=3\times72 .$$

Both products have the smaller factor first, and they do not match. So the size comparison on line III cannot rule
out a pairing such as $c-b=3$ and $c^{2}+cb+b^{2}=72$ with $a=6$. The simplest case that line III ignores is $c-b=1$.

There is no explicit counterexample with $a^{3}+b^{3}=c^{3}$, because the theorem is true. The point is that the step
**does not follow**, which is what makes a line of a proof wrong.

**Step 4 — Lines IV to VI.** These follow correctly from line III, but they inherit its error. So the first mistake
is line III.

**The idea.** A true theorem, a contradiction at the end, and neat algebra do not make a proof valid. A proof fails
at the first step that does not follow.
:::

| 8 | Tyler TMUA Set C · P2 Q3 | Reciprocals, an increasing function and an unknown multiplier |
| 9 | 2016 · P2 Q8 | Adding inequalities is safe; multiplying them is not |
| 10 | 2023 · P2 Q10 | A valid chain: dropping a half that is always true |
| 11 | Tyler TMUA Set C · P2 Q5 | A true statement with a proof that covers too little |
| 12 | Tyler TMUA Set D · P2 Q7 | A true theorem and a false step inside its proof |
| 13 | Notes on Logic and Proof · Exercise K, Q5 | A careless negation inside a contrapositive |
| 14 | Notes on Logic and Proof · Exercise O, Q1 | A proof that breaks when one number changes |
| 15 | 2020 · P2 Q8 | Judging a disproof: one counterexample is enough |
| 16 | 2023 · P2 Q4 | The exception hiding in "a multiple of 3, so not prime" |
